matched.set_b_axis: From self-authorizing knight to reconciled Christian self
matched.overlap_description: Both track a movement from self-made, mastery-seeking knightliness toward a more relational, humbled, and morally integrated final self.

matched.set_a_axis: From total chivalric misreading to partial lucid self-recognition
matched.set_b_axis: From impermeable enchantment to lucid renunciation
matched.overlap_description: Both describe a gradual loosening of delusion, culminating in explicit renunciation at the end, though B emphasizes final lucidity more strongly.

matched.set_a_axis: From invulnerable grandeur to wounded but self-restoring dignity
matched.set_b_axis: From heroic self-myth to repentant self-knowledge
matched.overlap_description: Both capture the collapse of grandiose self-image into a chastened, morally serious self-understanding.

matched.set_a_axis: From impulsive self-invention to disciplined moral obligation
matched.set_b_axis: From impulsive justice to disciplined moral judgment
matched.overlap_description: Both focus on the increasing formalization of his conduct from impulsive action toward rule-governed, ethically framed judgment and restraint.

unique_to_a.axis: From self-authoring knight to relationally embedded, chastened man
From total chivalric misreading to partial lucid self-recognition
From invulnerable grandeur to wounded but self-restoring dignity
From impulsive self-invention to disciplined moral obligation

unique_to_b.axis: From self-authorizing knight to reconciled Christian self
From impermeable enchantment to lucid renunciation
From heroic self-myth to repentant self-knowledge
From impulsive justice to disciplined moral judgment

matched.set_a_axis: From patronizing command to mutual dependence and affection
matched.set_b_axis: From patronizing recruitment to affectionate mutual dependence
matched.overlap_description: Both describe the Don Quixote–Sancho bond evolving from hierarchy into deep mutual reliance and affection.

matched.set_a_axis: From invented courtly admiration to absolute sustaining devotion
matched.set_b_axis: From fantasized lady to final moral center
matched.overlap_description: Both treat Dulcinea as a stable, idealized center of his identity whose importance deepens and persists to the end.

matched.set_a_axis: From honored guest to manipulated spectacle
matched.set_b_axis: From trusting hosts to exploited public spectacle
matched.overlap_description: Both see the duke and duchess as shifting from apparent validators of his knightly identity to agents of theatrical manipulation and humiliation.

unique_to_a.axis: From household ally to corrective opponent and back to partial reconciliation
From honored guest to manipulated spectacle

unique_to_b.axis: From friendly informant to hidden corrective adversary
From trusting hosts to exploited public spectacle

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From self-authorizing knight to reconciled Christian self
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Highly agentic self-assertion: he begins as a self-fashioning, mastery-seeking knight who imposes his will on reality, pursues fame, and treats others as supporting roles in his chivalric mission.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Communal, relationally embedded selfhood: he ends as Alonso Quixano, oriented toward confession, gratitude, family protection, and peaceful reconciliation with others and with God.

trajectory.position_description: He begins in maximal agency: he renames himself, arms himself, leaves home, recruits a squire, and insists on his own chivalric mission despite ridicule.
key_moments: Renames himself Don Quixote and Rocinante
Secures dubbing and begins sallying forth
Recruits Sancho Panza
Treats others as supporting roles in his quest

trajectory.position_description: Agency remains high but becomes increasingly mediated by others: he dominates interpretation, seeks public validation, and uses chivalric identity as a social performance while growing more dependent on Sancho and courtly audiences.
key_moments: Explains defeats as enchantment rather than error
Defends knight-errantry in long speeches
Advises Sancho on governance and conduct
Accepts courtly honors and public staging

trajectory.position_description: After defeat, his agency is sharply reduced and redirected inward: he submits to retirement, relinquishes the knightly self, and turns toward repentance, confession, and domestic responsibility.
key_moments: Defeated by the Knight of the White Moon
Returns home subdued and reflective
Makes his will and confesses
Renounces chivalric books and becomes Alonso Quixano the Good

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The arc moves from maximal self-assertion to a final state of humility, dependence, and relational repair. The middle of the novel preserves agency but increasingly socializes it, so the ending is best read as a genuine reorientation rather than a simple collapse.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From impermeable enchantment to lucid renunciation
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Fully enclosed in delusion: he treats romances as reality, misreads ordinary objects as enchanted signs, and explains contradiction through magic rather than self-correction.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Clear-eyed renunciation: he explicitly names his former madness, rejects chivalric books as harmful falsehoods, and recognizes his life as a moral error requiring repentance.

trajectory.position_description: He consistently converts the world into chivalric fantasy, with only tactical flexibility inside the delusion.
key_moments: Inn becomes castle
Windmills become giants
Defeats are explained as enchantment
Sierra Morena penance is treated as literal chivalric performance

trajectory.position_description: He remains deluded, but the delusion is increasingly staged, publicly manipulated, and occasionally tested by practical reality; he sometimes notices facts, but absorbs them back into enchantment.
key_moments: Courtly pranks and staged enchantments at the duke's castle
Cave of Montesinos and Clavileño intensify wonder without correction
He can occasionally distinguish local realities from fantasy
He preserves his worldview by reclassifying contradictions

trajectory.position_description: The delusional system collapses into explicit renunciation; he sees his former self as mad and rejects knight-errantry as deception.
key_moments: Defeat by the Knight of the White Moon
Melancholy retreat home
Confession and will-making
Renounces Don Quixote and becomes Alonso Quixano

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: This is the clearest psychological arc in the material: from complete enchantment-thinking to a final repudiation of that worldview. The middle chapters show resilient, adaptive delusion rather than true realism, making the ending a decisive break.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From heroic self-myth to repentant self-knowledge
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Grandiose self-mythologizing: he imagines himself as a legendary knight, equal to or greater than famous heroes, destined for fame and kingship.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Repentant humility: he sees himself as a sinner who must die as a good Christian and leave behind the vanity of heroic self-invention.

trajectory.position_description: He repeatedly enlarges himself through comparison to epic and chivalric figures, treating injuries as proof of greatness.
key_moments: Claims kinship with the Twelve Peers and Nine Worthies
Treats defeats as ordinary knightly setbacks
Imagines future kingship and marriage to a princess
Adopts exalted knightly titles

trajectory.position_description: Grandiosity becomes more polished and socially legible: he speaks as a public authority, a moral teacher, and a famous knight whose life is already in print.
key_moments: Defends arms over letters
Argues about his own literary fame
Uses public recognition in Barcelona as proof of identity
Accepts courtly honors as confirmation of greatness

trajectory.position_description: He abandons heroic inflation and adopts humility, repentance, and Christian self-assessment.
key_moments: Renounces chivalric books
Calls himself Alonso Quixano the Good
Makes his will and seeks forgiveness

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Don Quixote begins with inflated heroic self-conception and ends with explicit humility. The middle of the novel does not eliminate grandiosity so much as refine it into a socially performative, publicly validated self-image before the final collapse.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From impulsive justice to disciplined moral judgment
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Impulsive, fantasy-driven justice: he acts immediately on perceived wrongs, with little distinction between appearance and fact.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Disciplined moral judgment: he becomes capable of practical counsel, legal distinction, and Christian self-governance.

trajectory.position_description: He rushes into moral action on the basis of delusion, often worsening the situation.
key_moments: Forces Juan Haldudo to promise justice
Attacks the galley slaves
Intervenes in the sheep and procession episodes

trajectory.position_description: He increasingly speaks as a moral philosopher and practical adviser, especially on arms, governance, and honor.
key_moments: Defense of arms over letters
Advice to Sancho on governing Barataria
Long moral counsel on justice, mercy, and prudence

trajectory.position_description: His final state is one of explicit moral accounting: confession, repentance, will-making, and concern for the souls and futures of others.
key_moments: Stops Sancho's lashes when they seem excessive
Makes his will and settles accounts
Protects niece and household from chivalric corruption

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: This axis captures the increasing seriousness of his ethical life: from reckless intervention to a more disciplined, if still idealized, moral judgment, culminating in Christian repentance and practical responsibility.

relational_axes.axis_name: From patronizing recruitment to affectionate mutual dependence
relational_axes.pole_start: He begins by recruiting Sancho as a subordinate squire, treating him as useful, persuadable, and intellectually inferior within the chivalric hierarchy.
relational_axes.pole_end: He ends as a grateful, affectionate companion who recognizes Sancho's fidelity, values his practical wisdom, and rewards him with explicit care and acknowledgment.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho is useful, promising, and subordinate; Don Quixote patronizes him, promises him rewards, and expects obedience.
key_moments: Promises Sancho an island or kingdom
Uses Sancho as messenger and witness
Rebukes Sancho's skepticism and proverbs

trajectory.position_description: Their bond deepens into a mix of affection, irritation, and dependence; Don Quixote increasingly relies on Sancho's practical help while still asserting superiority.
key_moments: Sancho becomes a constant companion through courtly and pastoral episodes
Don Quixote alternates between scolding and praising him
He entrusts Sancho with governance and moral instruction
He depends on Sancho for travel, interpretation, and emotional steadiness

trajectory.position_description: The relationship becomes more openly tender and reciprocal: Don Quixote blesses Sancho, worries about him, protects him from humiliation, and finally settles accounts while acknowledging his fidelity.
key_moments: Tears at Sancho's departure for Barataria
Protects him from excessive self-scourging
Thanks him and settles accounts at the end
Final repentance includes concern for Sancho's future

relational_axes.evidence_summary: This is the richest relationship arc in the novel: it moves from hierarchy to intimacy, from comic mismatch to genuine mutual attachment. Don Quixote never stops being the master, but by the end he is also deeply dependent on and emotionally attached to Sancho.

relational_axes.axis_name: From fantasized lady to final moral center
relational_axes.pole_start: She begins as a wholly fantasized courtly beloved, an abstract lady who legitimizes his knightly identity.
relational_axes.pole_end: She ends as the enduring moral and emotional center of his life, even as he renounces knight-errantry and repents.

trajectory.position_description: Dulcinea is the imagined source of his mission, honor, and courtly language; she is intensely idealized but not yet morally tested.
key_moments: Transforms Aldonza Lorenzo into Dulcinea
Invokes her in first combats
Uses her as the standard for all chivalric action

trajectory.position_description: She becomes the fixed center of his identity, the justification for penance, resistance to temptation, and all public self-presentation.
key_moments: Sierra Morena penance
Refusal of Altisidora
Dulcinea's disenchantment becomes the engine of the later plot
He repeatedly insists on her exclusivity and beauty

trajectory.position_description: Even as he renounces chivalry, Dulcinea remains the beloved whose memory structures his repentance and final moral order.
key_moments: Refuses to deny her beauty in the duel
Continues to seek her disenchantment after defeat
Dies as Alonso Quixano while still honoring her place in his life

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Dulcinea never becomes a real interpersonal relationship, but she becomes the deepest organizing attachment in his psyche. The arc is less about change in feeling than about increasing moral centrality, surviving even the collapse of his knightly identity.

relational_axes.axis_name: From honored guest to manipulated spectacle
relational_axes.pole_start: He initially experiences the duke and duchess as noble patrons who recognize and elevate his knightly identity.
relational_axes.pole_end: He ends as a guest who still receives courtesy, but who increasingly understands, at least dimly, that their hospitality is also theatrical manipulation and mockery.

trajectory.position_description: The duke and duchess stage elaborate honors that make Don Quixote feel authentically knightly and socially visible.
key_moments: Ceremonial reception at the castle
Public honors and deference
Don Quixote feels truly recognized

trajectory.position_description: Their hospitality becomes increasingly prankish: Sancho is mocked, Altisidora is staged, and Don Quixote is repeatedly made part of a comic performance.
key_moments: Pranks on Sancho
Altisidora's mock love
Clavileño and other staged marvels

trajectory.position_description: He remains courteous, but the courtly environment now feels more conditional and cruel. He is humiliated, confined, and increasingly aware that noble hospitality can mask exploitation.
key_moments: Doña Rodriguez episode
Public humiliation and confinement
Departure from the castle after defeat

relational_axes.evidence_summary: This relationship is not a simple betrayal arc; it is a shift from sincere-seeming honor to elaborate social theater. Don Quixote remains deferential, but the emotional tone moves from validation to wary endurance.

relational_axes.axis_name: From household ally to corrective opponent and back to partial reconciliation
relational_axes.pole_start: He begins with the curate as a familiar village authority, not yet an enemy, though already outside his fantasy world.
relational_axes.pole_end: He ends with a more cordial, socially integrated relation, even though the curate remains a manager of his sanity and narrative.

trajectory.position_description: The curate is still part of the household circle, but his role shifts sharply when he helps burn the books and diagnose Don Quixote's madness.
key_moments: Household diagnoses his condition
Curate resolves to burn the books
Book-burning begins

trajectory.position_description: The curate becomes a visible agent of containment, judgment, and manipulation. Don Quixote senses condemnation, especially when his galley-slave episode and madness are discussed.
key_moments: Curate mentions the galley slaves
Public discussion of his madness
Curate participates in the cage deception

trajectory.position_description: The curate is now a learned interlocutor whose skepticism Don Quixote resists, though the exchange is often courteous and serious rather than openly hostile.
key_moments: Canon and curate criticize chivalric books
Don Quixote defends knight-errantry
The curate listens and sometimes validates his reasoning

trajectory.position_description: By the end, the curate is again a trusted village figure. Don Quixote greets him affectionately and accepts his care, even as he renounces the old fantasy life.
key_moments: Warm return to the village
Accepts advice and care
Dies reconciled within the household

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The curate's relationship with Don Quixote moves from domestic familiarity to corrective antagonism and then to a softened, reintegrated ending. He is one of the main external forces trying to cure him, but the final chapters restore social trust.

matched.set_a_axis: From dependent squire to self-directed negotiator
matched.set_b_axis: From dependent squirely attachment to self-possessed practical agency
matched.overlap_description: Both describe Sancho's movement from relational dependence and opportunistic service toward stronger self-direction, bargaining power, and practical autonomy without severing loyalty.

matched.set_a_axis: From practical disbelief to strategic participation in fantasy
matched.set_b_axis: From credulous opportunism to hardened practical skepticism
matched.overlap_description: Both track Sancho's evolving relation to belief: he begins as a realist who doubts Quixote, then learns to perform or use fantasy tactically while retaining underlying skepticism.

matched.set_a_axis: From bodily comfort to dignified self-respect
matched.set_b_axis: From comic rustic to self-conscious public figure
matched.overlap_description: Both capture Sancho's rise in self-regard: he remains materially minded, but increasingly cares about dignity, reputation, and how he is publicly seen.

unique_to_a.axis: From comic peasant to capable public figure

unique_to_b.axis: From credulous opportunism to hardened practical skepticism

matched.set_a_axis: From hopeful faith to wary, negotiated loyalty
matched.set_b_axis: From opportunistic follower to affectionate, skeptical companion
matched.overlap_description: Both describe the central Sancho-Quixote bond as moving from reward-based attachment to a durable companionship marked by skepticism, bargaining, and continued loyalty.

matched.set_a_axis: From private husband to ambitious family negotiator
matched.set_b_axis: From practical spouse to family-centered status negotiator
matched.overlap_description: Both treat Teresa Panza as the domestic counterpart to Sancho's ambitions, showing a shift from private household obligation to negotiated family advancement.

matched.set_a_axis: From practical possession to emotional companion
matched.set_b_axis: From practical mount to beloved companion and symbol of freedom
matched.overlap_description: Both see Dapple evolving from utility into an emotionally charged companion tied to Sancho's identity, comfort, and homecoming.

matched.set_a_axis: From wary dependence to grateful but guarded favor
matched.set_b_axis: From wary dependence to grateful, tactical attachment
matched.overlap_description: Both characterize Sancho's relation to the Duchess as one of useful patronage mixed with manipulation, ending in gratitude tempered by caution.

unique_to_a.axis: From admiration for a master to respect mixed with criticism
From useful informant to object of educated mockery

unique_to_b.axis: From hopeful patronage to wary instrumentalism

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From dependent squire to self-possessed practical negotiator
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Sancho begins strongly communion-leaning: he attaches himself to Don Quixote for reward, companionship, and shared adventure, with his identity largely defined by service and dependence.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He ends with stronger agency while remaining relationally attached: he can govern, bargain, resist coercion, set limits, and define himself as Sancho rather than as a mere appendage to Quixote.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho joins Quixote for promised advancement, but the bond is still marked by trust, deference, and opportunistic hope.
key_moments: Accepts the island promise and sets out as squire
Balances hope with practical jokes about family and comfort
Already shows a practical self-interest that will later support agency

trajectory.position_description: Repeated beatings, hunger, and danger push Sancho toward self-protective agency. He stays attached, but increasingly negotiates, corrects, and manages risk rather than simply following.
key_moments: Warns Quixote about real danger and bodily consequences
Bargains over wages, balsam, and rewards
Plans conditional withdrawal while continuing to serve

trajectory.position_description: Sancho becomes more self-conscious about his public image and more willing to manage deception. He shapes narratives around Dulcinea, his own ambitions, and the printed story of his adventures.
key_moments: Learns his story is in print and reacts defensively
Uses the false Dulcinea scheme strategically
Speaks more openly about his own limits and prospects

trajectory.position_description: Sancho reaches a peak of agency in Barataria: he governs, judges, resists humiliation, and insists on his own identity and limits.
key_moments: Accepts and performs the governorship
Issues practical judgments and ordinances
Rejects the office when it becomes unsustainable

trajectory.position_description: After abandoning office, Sancho does not become passive again; instead, he chooses a more mature dependence on Quixote, grounded in clearer self-knowledge and stronger boundaries.
key_moments: Rejects further ambition in favor of ordinary life
Returns to Quixote by choice
Mourns Quixote's death with genuine attachment

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho's arc moves from relationally driven dependence toward a more self-possessed practical agency that still values communion. He ends more autonomous in judgment, but not less attached.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From practical disbelief to strategic, hardened skepticism
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Sancho begins as a commonsense realist who sees Quixote's world as deluded and dangerous, though he is willing to entertain the promises enough to join the adventure.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He ends deeply skeptical of enchantment, chivalric interpretation, and courtly fantasy, while still able to perform belief tactically when it serves survival, loyalty, or profit.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho accepts the island fantasy enough to follow, but his realism is already present as comic skepticism.
key_moments: Believes in promised island or governorship
Jokes about his wife's suitability for queenship
Warns Quixote about ordinary reality

trajectory.position_description: Beatings, legal danger, and obvious misreadings make Sancho more skeptical and more insistent on bodily evidence.
key_moments: Recognizes the cost of Quixote's delusions
Insists windmills and friars are ordinary things
Treats pain and punishment as real

trajectory.position_description: Sancho no longer believes fantasy as truth, but he participates in it as a practical strategy, using enchantment language when it helps him survive or profit.
key_moments: Calls Dulcinea a village woman while maintaining the fiction
Uses enchantment explanations to manage Quixote
Insists on bodily evidence against illusions

trajectory.position_description: Sancho's skepticism becomes experiential and durable: he knows what office, pain, and public performance really cost, and he is no longer tempted by fantasy as belief.
key_moments: Rejects governorship as his true calling after experiencing it
Treats omens and courtly games as practical nonsense
Returns home-oriented and materially grounded

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho moves from partial credulity to a mature skepticism that still allows tactical participation. His realism remains stable, but it becomes sharper and more explicit over time.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From comic rustic to self-conscious public figure
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Sancho begins as an earthy peasant squire whose identity is defined by appetite, wit, and service, and who is still largely subject to ridicule.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He ends as a self-aware public person who knows his name, reputation, and role in print, and who actively manages how he is seen.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho is bodily, practical, and only modestly reflective. He knows what he wants, but not yet how others will narrate him.
key_moments: Prefers bread, onions, food, and comfort
Defines himself as peaceful and practical
Already senses his low social position

trajectory.position_description: Learning that his adventures are being written changes Sancho's self-conception. He becomes aware of being watched, judged, and represented.
key_moments: Discovers the printed history
Objects to misrepresentation
Begins shaping his own story through letters and speeches

trajectory.position_description: As governor, Sancho insists on being Sancho Panza, not a false nobleman. He understands that clothing and office are performances, and he tries to control the image.
key_moments: Rejects the honorific 'Don'
Uses letters to Teresa to manage family identity
Defends his reputation against false histories

trajectory.position_description: At the end, Sancho is fully aware of his bodily limits, his love of comfort, and his deep attachment to Quixote. He is no longer merely comic; he is self-defining in grief and loyalty.
key_moments: Negotiates the whipping as labor
Returns homeward-oriented and identity-conscious
Mourns Quixote's death with genuine emotional dependence

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho rises from rustic comic function to a figure who knows he is being narrated, judged, and remembered. He becomes increasingly able to speak for himself and defend his identity.

relational_axes.axis_name: From opportunistic follower to affectionate, skeptical companion
relational_axes.pole_start: Sancho begins as a hopeful dependent who follows Don Quixote mainly for promised reward and social mobility, with limited emotional attachment.
relational_axes.pole_end: He ends as a deeply attached companion who still doubts Quixote's interpretations, but whose loyalty is grounded in affection, shared history, and chosen companionship rather than mere profit.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho follows Quixote because he believes the knight can advance him. Trust is high, intimacy moderate, and skepticism still relatively mild.
key_moments: Accepts the island promise
Accompanies Quixote as squire
Tests promises through conversation

trajectory.position_description: Repeated harm makes Sancho more skeptical and more openly corrective, but he remains attached and continues to manage Quixote rather than leave him.
key_moments: Warns Quixote about real danger
Argues against enchantment explanations
Continues to follow despite beatings and humiliation

trajectory.position_description: Sancho becomes more openly transactional and self-assertive, but the relationship also deepens through shared public life, letters, and the governorship. He is both more critical and more intimate.
key_moments: Defends his own reputation in print
Uses Quixote's fantasy for his own advancement
Returns to Quixote after Barataria with renewed attachment

trajectory.position_description: After Quixote's defeat and death, Sancho's skepticism remains, but his emotional dependence becomes unmistakable. He grieves, pleads, and tries to keep the bond alive through pastoral plans.
key_moments: Mourns Quixote's defeat
Tries to keep him alive and hopeful
Weeps at his deathbed and resists losing him

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho's central relationship arc moves from self-interested service to a durable, emotionally rich bond in which skepticism and affection coexist. He never stops seeing Quixote as mad, but he increasingly loves him as a person.

relational_axes.axis_name: From practical spouse to family-centered status negotiator
relational_axes.pole_start: Teresa is initially a beloved but realistically bounded wife, someone Sancho affectionately imagines benefiting from his rise but not yet a major site of social negotiation.
relational_axes.pole_end: By the end, Teresa is a full partner in Sancho's social imagination: he writes to her, plans for her status, and frames his ambitions around family advancement and homecoming.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho thinks of Teresa with affection and realism, doubting her fitness for queenship but imagining her as a countess or beneficiary of his rise.
key_moments: Says his wife is not fit to be queen
Imagines children benefiting from advancement
Keeps family in the background of his ambitions

trajectory.position_description: Teresa becomes a more active presence as Sancho writes to her, boasts to her, and imagines her reaction to his prospects.
key_moments: Speaks to Teresa about his adventures
Uses family as justification for ambition
Begins to think in terms of household uplift

trajectory.position_description: Teresa becomes central to Sancho's social project. He wants her to understand rank, accept his ambitions, and share in the material and symbolic benefits of office.
key_moments: Argues with Teresa about rank and reputation
Sends letters and gifts home
Frames governorship as family advancement

trajectory.position_description: Teresa is no longer just a beneficiary of ambition but the emotional anchor of Sancho's return. His desires settle into domesticity, and his bond with her becomes more grounded and reciprocal.
key_moments: Rejects further office and returns homeward
Corresponds with Teresa as a real partner in status
Ends with grief and home-centered loyalty

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Teresa is the main relational anchor for Sancho's domestic and social aspirations. Over time, she shifts from background spouse to active partner in his identity as a man seeking dignity, money, and a stable home.

relational_axes.axis_name: From practical mount to beloved companion and symbol of freedom
relational_axes.pole_start: Dapple begins as Sancho's practical means of travel and a sign of his peasant identity.
relational_axes.pole_end: Dapple ends as emotionally central: a companion, a symbol of home and freedom, and something Sancho protects with genuine affection.

trajectory.position_description: Dapple is mainly a useful ass, part of Sancho's material equipment and mobility.
key_moments: Prepares for travel with ass and alforjas
Uses Dapple as practical transport
Values him as part of ordinary life

trajectory.position_description: Loss or threat to Dapple becomes a real grievance. Sancho's attachment becomes visibly affectionate and possessive.
key_moments: Rages over Dapple's theft
Treats the ass as a symbol of security
Worries about Dapple's welfare

trajectory.position_description: Dapple becomes a stable emotional anchor, especially during the governorship and the return home. Sancho repeatedly worries about his comfort and safety.
key_moments: Protects Dapple in courtly and military settings
Uses Dapple as a marker of his true identity
Treats him as part of home and freedom

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Dapple evolves from utility to intimacy. The donkey becomes a piece of Sancho's selfhood, domestic life, and freedom from aristocratic fantasy.

relational_axes.axis_name: From wary dependence to grateful, tactical attachment
relational_axes.pole_start: Sancho initially sees the Duchess as a powerful noble patron whose favor can be useful but whose games are suspect.
relational_axes.pole_end: He remains wary of her manipulation but is genuinely grateful for her protection and attention, and he has learned to navigate her favor tactically.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho is dazzled by the Duchess's courtesy and sees her as a source of status, but he is already aware that the castle is theatrical and manipulative.
key_moments: Feels validated by her recognition
Enjoys noble hospitality
Begins to see patronage as useful

trajectory.position_description: Sancho becomes more dependent on the Duchess's favor while also feeling humiliated by courtly jokes and coercion.
key_moments: Resents humiliating courtly pranks
Bargains over the governorship and Dulcinea
Uses the Duchess's attention to protect his standing

trajectory.position_description: Sancho learns to work within the Duchess's system, speaking more freely while still seeking her protection. He is less dazzled and more strategic.
key_moments: Handles the Trifaldi and Clavileño episodes tactically
Negotiates the governorship and penance
Writes to Teresa under noble supervision

trajectory.position_description: After Barataria and later courtly humiliations, Sancho is less enchanted by the Duchess but still grateful for the social capital her world provides.
key_moments: Rejects governorship as a burden after the prank
Returns to the castle world with caution
Treats noble favor as useful but not trustworthy

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The Duchess is a major relational axis because she repeatedly offers Sancho status, protection, and humiliation at once. His relation to her evolves from dazzled opportunism to a more mature, guarded dependence.

matched.set_a_axis: From absent object to externally imposed symbolic communion
matched.set_b_axis: From absent projection to mediated relational symbol
matched.overlap_description: Both describe Dulcinea as lacking independent interiority and becoming increasingly defined through others' projections, especially as a symbolic relational figure rather than an autonomous self.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From absent projection to mediated relational symbol
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Purely an externally constructed ideal: no independent agency, no self-assertion, and no direct consciousness; she exists only as a projected beloved.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Still largely non-agentic, but increasingly framed as a relational symbol with a mediated social function in Don Quixote's fantasies and the courtly prank machinery.

trajectory.position_description: Dulcinea is introduced only through Don Quixote's renaming and devotion. She has no direct speech, action, or self-awareness, and remains an absent object of projection rather than a participating subject.
key_moments: Aldonza Lorenzo is renamed Dulcinea del Toboso
She is repeatedly invoked as the recipient of vows and praise
No independent interiority is shown

trajectory.position_description: Her image becomes more socially embedded as Sancho, the duke and duchess, and Don Quixote use her name strategically. She is still non-agentic, but now functions as a shared symbolic reference point in comic and chivalric performance.
key_moments: Sancho fabricates replies and uses her name pragmatically
The duke and duchess exploit her image in courtly deception
Don Quixote's enchantment narrative makes her a public symbol

trajectory.position_description: She is briefly given a performed voice in the disenchantment pageant, but this remains externally scripted. The novel ends with her still fundamentally dependent on others' projections and not truly agentic.
key_moments: Merlin's pageant voices a distressed Dulcinea
The disenchantment plot makes her the object of Sancho's penance
Later chapters continue to invoke her as Don Quixote's final ideal

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Dulcinea shows almost no genuine intrapersonal development because she is not sustained as an interior consciousness in the novel. Across the text, she remains overwhelmingly communion-defined and relationally constructed, with no independent agency emerging.

relational_axes.axis_name: From imagined beloved to narrated cause of action
relational_axes.pole_start: A purely idealized beloved who exists only as the object of Don Quixote's devotion and fantasy.
relational_axes.pole_end: A more elaborately mediated symbolic partner whose name organizes his vows, penance, suffering, and final renunciation, though still without reciprocal consciousness.

trajectory.position_description: Dulcinea is entirely a projection of Don Quixote's chivalric imagination; the relationship is one-way devotion with no evidence of her own response.
key_moments: Her name is created and elevated by Don Quixote
She is invoked as the source of his courage and suffering
No direct reciprocity is shown

trajectory.phase: Instrument of vows, penance, and public action
trajectory.position_description: Her role expands as Don Quixote uses her name to authorize actions, justify penance, and interpret enchantment. She becomes the organizing center of his self-conception and public conduct.
key_moments: Letters and messages are addressed to her
Her supposed enchantment motivates schemes involving Don Quixote and Sancho
Courtly figures exploit her name in staged deceptions

trajectory.phase: Enchantment, rescue fantasy, and final reaffirmation
trajectory.position_description: She remains the final and exclusive beloved, now tied to disenchantment, suffering, and deathbed renunciation. The relationship is still one-sided but more emotionally charged and terminal.
key_moments: The pageant and disenchantment plot center on her
Sancho's lashes are meant to restore her
Don Quixote's final vows and renunciation still orbit her name

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The relationship with Don Quixote is the only one with sustained significance, but it is structurally one-sided throughout. Dulcinea never becomes an autonomous partner; she remains the imagined beloved whose symbolic function deepens over time.

relational_axes.axis_name: From absent ideal to manipulated emblem
relational_axes.pole_start: An absent, unknown lady whose existence is only meaningful through Don Quixote's fantasy.
relational_axes.pole_end: A heavily manipulated emblem used by Sancho for practical jokes, bargaining, and the disenchantment plot, still without any direct reciprocal relation.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho knows her only as Don Quixote's lady; she is a distant name with no direct relational content.
key_moments: Sancho hears and repeats her name
He contrasts her with Aldonza Lorenzo
No direct relationship exists

trajectory.position_description: Sancho increasingly uses her name in letters, lies, and bargaining, while also being drawn into responsibility for her supposed condition. She becomes a tool within his comic pragmatism and a burden imposed by the enchantment story.
key_moments: Sancho fabricates replies
He leverages her name to manage Don Quixote
Merlin frames her restoration as dependent on Sancho's penance

trajectory.position_description: She becomes the explicit justification for Sancho's lashes and the central token in the enchantment/disenchantment bargain. The connection remains external, coercive, and non-mutual, even as it is used for comic pressure and narrative leverage.
key_moments: Merlin's pageant speaks in her name
Sancho is pressured to scourge himself for her restoration
Her name remains a practical and comic lever

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho's relation to Dulcinea is not intimate but instrumental. Over time, he moves from merely repeating her name to actively manipulating it, yet this is a change in use rather than in mutual relationship.

relational_axes.axis_name: From literary reference to theatrical prop
relational_axes.pole_start: A literary and chivalric reference point known only through Don Quixote's story.
relational_axes.pole_end: A theatrical prop in the duke and duchess's elaborate mockery, used to stage enchantment, rivalry, and social performance.

trajectory.position_description: The duke and duchess treat Dulcinea as part of the Don Quixote legend, using her name to frame their amusement and courtly play.
key_moments: They discuss and praise her in conversation
Her identity is folded into their knowledge of Don Quixote
She becomes a topic for social performance

trajectory.position_description: Her image is staged, impersonated, and weaponized in the enchantment/disenchantment plot, making her a tool of aristocratic manipulation rather than a person.
key_moments: Merlin's pageant presents a voiced Dulcinea
The duchess uses her name to sustain the prank
Her supposed condition becomes part of the court's spectacle

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The duke and duchess do not relate to Dulcinea as a person but as a narrative device. Their interaction is best understood as exploitation of her symbolic value for entertainment and control.

matched.set_a_axis: From playful social mediator to wounded but morally invested reformer
matched.set_b_axis: From detached strategist to restrained co-witness
matched.overlap_description: Both describe Carrasco moving from witty, socially agile manipulation toward a more restrained, morally serious, and closure-oriented stance by the end.

matched.set_a_axis: From self-assured wit to wounded resolve
matched.set_b_axis: From self-assured planner to chastened but persistent reformer
matched.overlap_description: Both track a fall from confidence into humiliation after defeat, followed by a tempered, experience-earned persistence rather than simple collapse.

matched.set_a_axis: From ironic manipulation to commemorative respect
matched.set_b_axis: From amused skepticism to practical acceptance of limits
matched.overlap_description: Both capture a late softening: Carrasco moves away from comic distance and toward acceptance of Don Quixote's final reality, with respect replacing mockery.

unique_to_a.axis: From ironic manipulation to commemorative respect

unique_to_b.axis: From amused skepticism to practical acceptance of limits

matched.overlap_description: Both describe the Carrasco-Don Quixote relationship as beginning in covert control and ending in respectful, deathbed recognition and memorialization.

matched.set_a_axis: From incidental banter to limited esteem
matched.set_b_axis: From comic patronage to cautious respect
matched.overlap_description: Both identify a modest but real arc with Sancho: from banter and asymmetry toward practical recognition and limited esteem.

unique_to_a.axis: From incidental banter to limited esteem

unique_to_b.axis: From comic patronage to cautious respect

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From witty manipulator to restrained co-witness
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Begins as a socially agile, self-assertive strategist who uses wit, flattery, and disguise to manage Don Quixote from a position of interpretive control.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Ends as a more restrained, morally serious participant who still acts decisively but is oriented toward witness, humane closure, and respect rather than domination.

trajectory.position_description: Carrasco is socially embedded and verbally agile, enjoying the role of witty intermediary while also setting events in motion behind the scenes.
key_moments: Chapter 55: introduced as the learned bachelor who brings news of the printed history
Chapters 56-57: flattery, debate, and conversational steering
Chapter 60: helps arrange Don Quixote's departure through a hidden plan
Chapter 61: his influence becomes partly offstage after the scheme is launched

trajectory.position_description: His agency remains strong, but humiliation after the failed disguise and defeat makes his control more reactive, embittered, and less triumphant.
key_moments: Chapter 67: the Knight of the Mirrors scheme is exposed
Chapter 68: he is beaten, humiliated, and turns failure into renewed resolve

trajectory.position_description: In the later chapters, he remains active but increasingly channels his agency into containment, accommodation, and finally solemn witness at Don Quixote's death.
key_moments: Chapter 103: skeptical investigation of Sancho's governorship
Chapter 105: continued doubt about Sancho's political rise
Chapter 118: returns as the chastened Knight of the White Moon
Chapter 126: tactically accommodates the pastoral scheme
Chapter 127: witnesses Don Quixote's lucid death and helps close the story

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Both analyses agree that Carrasco is fundamentally agentic, but his agency changes in quality: from playful control to wounded persistence, then into a more restrained and socially accountable form of participation.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From self-assured planner to chastened but persistent reformer
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Starts as a highly self-assured planner who believes wit, disguise, and tactical orchestration can control Don Quixote and shape events.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Ends more chastened and realistic, aware of the limits of intervention, yet still committed to reform and closure.

trajectory.position_description: He acts as though his intelligence and social skill are sufficient to manage the situation, showing little doubt about his competence.
key_moments: Chapters 56-57: witty control of conversation
Chapter 60: orchestrates Don Quixote's departure through a hidden plan

trajectory.position_description: The failed staged defeat forces him into a humbler posture, making clear that planning is easier than execution and that Quixote's interpretive world can defeat strategy.
key_moments: Chapter 67: Don Quixote identifies him despite the disguise
Chapter 68: he is bruised, frustrated, and more tactically realistic

trajectory.position_description: He remains committed, but his confidence is moderated by failure; by the end he functions more as a serious manager of closure than a triumphant mastermind.
key_moments: Chapter 118: defeat as the Knight of the White Moon confirms both persistence and failure
Chapter 126: accommodates Don Quixote's pastoral fantasy
Chapter 127: helps close the story with restraint and seriousness

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The merged evidence shows a clear arc from confident control into chastened competence. Carrasco does not abandon his reformist project, but he loses the illusion that cleverness alone guarantees success.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From amused skepticism to practical acceptance
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Begins skeptical, amused, and somewhat detached, treating the Quixote world as something to analyze, mock, or manage from the outside.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Ends in practical acceptance of what cannot be controlled, especially once death and closure supersede further manipulation.

trajectory.position_description: He doubts Sancho's governorship and treats the surrounding events as theatrical, dubious, or enchantment-like, with lively comic skepticism.
key_moments: Chapter 103: astonished curiosity about Sancho's letters and gifts
Chapter 105: reported doubt about Sancho's governorship

trajectory.position_description: He continues to interpret events rationally, but repeated failure makes his skepticism more pragmatic than playful, and he increasingly accommodates what he cannot reverse.
key_moments: Chapter 118: corrective intervention against Don Quixote
Chapter 126: accepts the pastoral scheme to keep Don Quixote home

trajectory.position_description: At the deathbed, skepticism yields to acceptance of the ordinary final truth of Don Quixote's death, and Carrasco helps certify closure rather than prolong interpretive contest.
key_moments: Chapter 127: witnesses the death and helps secure the official ending

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Carrasco never stops being skeptical, but his skepticism becomes less comic and more practical. The final movement is toward acceptance of limits and the end of intervention.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From playful irony to solemn containment
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Starts playful, teasing, and socially witty, using irony as a mode of control and performance.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: Ends sober, restrained, and funerary in tone, using composure to contain grief and finalize Don Quixote's story.

trajectory.position_description: He enjoys verbal play, flattery, and comic management of others; irony is his main social tool.
key_moments: Chapters 56-57: witty conversation and teasing
Chapter 60: playful but manipulative encouragement of Don Quixote

trajectory.position_description: His irony remains, but it is shadowed by humiliation and anger; the comic mask does not disappear, but it becomes less carefree.
key_moments: Chapter 68: he is physically hurt and meditates vengeance

trajectory.position_description: The final chapter places him in a serious, restrained role, no longer as a prankish strategist but as a witness to death and guardian of narrative finality.
key_moments: Chapter 127: bedside witness, will-management, epitaph, and closure

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: This axis is a useful supplement from the psychological summary: it isolates the tonal shift from comic irony to grave responsibility, which is present in the event-based material but not fully foregrounded there.

relational_axes.axis_name: From manipulative management to chastened respect
relational_axes.pole_start: Begins as a clever manipulator who sees Don Quixote as a problem to be managed through disguise, performance, and strategic deception.
relational_axes.pole_end: Ends with respect and pity, treating Don Quixote as a dignified, suffering man whose death should be witnessed and honored, even while Carrasco still wants the official story to close on his terms.

trajectory.position_description: He flatters and manages Don Quixote, keeping him engaged while secretly advancing a plan.
key_moments: Chapters 56-57: witty flattery and conversational steering
Chapter 60: pretends to encourage the third sally while actually orchestrating it

trajectory.position_description: The Knight of the Mirrors scheme turns the relationship openly adversarial, though still framed as correction rather than hatred.
key_moments: Chapter 67: Don Quixote recognizes him despite the disguise
Chapter 68: Carrasco is humiliated and becomes more determined

trajectory.position_description: He now sees Don Quixote as someone to be cured and returned home, not merely outwitted; his intervention becomes more paternal and containment-oriented.
key_moments: Chapter 118: the Knight of the White Moon defeat is meant to force retirement
Chapter 126: he accommodates the pastoral fantasy to keep Don Quixote home

trajectory.position_description: At death, the relationship softens into respectful witness. He helps define Don Quixote as Alonso Quixano, sane and finished.
key_moments: Chapter 127: bedside presence, will, repentance, and death

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Carrasco's relationship with Don Quixote moves from covert control to failed correction, then to paternalistic containment and finally respectful memorialization. The final chapters decisively reframe the relationship.

relational_axes.axis_name: From comic patronage to cautious respect
relational_axes.pole_start: Initially treats Sancho as a comic subordinate or amusing interlocutor, engaging him with wit and some condescension.
relational_axes.pole_end: Ends with cautious, practical respect for Sancho as part of the shared effort to contain Don Quixote, though the relationship remains lightly comic rather than intimate.

trajectory.position_description: He jokes with Sancho and treats him as a comic equal worth sparring with verbally.
key_moments: Chapters 56-57: good-humored teasing and quick wit

trajectory.position_description: He is surprised by Sancho's bargaining and practical seriousness, which slightly increases his recognition of Sancho's intelligence even while he remains patronizing.
key_moments: Chapter 60: surprise at Sancho's comic seriousness
Chapter 68: aftermath of the scheme keeps Sancho in the orbit of practical maneuvering

trajectory.position_description: Sancho becomes a figure whose letters, governorship, grief, and practical role must be taken seriously, even if Carrasco never becomes emotionally intimate with him.
key_moments: Chapter 103: investigates Sancho's governorship through letters and testimony
Chapter 105: continues to doubt the governorship while engaging with it
Chapter 127: Sancho's grief is part of the shared deathbed scene

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Carrasco's relation to Sancho stays comic and indirect, but it develops from teasing condescension toward practical recognition of Sancho's intelligence and usefulness. This is a modest relational arc, not a deep emotional bond.

relational_axes.axis_name: From conspiratorial alliance to stable coordination
relational_axes.pole_start: Begins already aligned with the curate and barber in the project of controlling Don Quixote.
relational_axes.pole_end: Ends still aligned, with the alliance remaining stable and functional rather than emotionally deepening.

trajectory.position_description: He works with them to stage Don Quixote's departure and maintain the larger plan.
key_moments: Chapter 60: the departure is arranged through a hidden scheme
Chapter 61: the plan continues offstage

trajectory.position_description: The alliance remains tactically useful as Carrasco returns in disguise to force Don Quixote's retirement.
key_moments: Chapter 118: the Knight of the White Moon defeat
Chapter 123: retrospective explanation of the duke's plot and Carrasco's role

trajectory.position_description: The broader network of management culminates in the orderly deathbed ending, with Carrasco still socially coordinated with the household's closure.
key_moments: Chapter 127: will, confession, and final witness

relational_axes.evidence_summary: This relationship is stable rather than transformative, but it matters because it supports Carrasco's agency. The curate and barber remain his practical collaborators throughout the anti-Quixote project.

matched.set_a_axis: From aristocratic spectatorship to collaborative theatrical mastery
matched.set_b_axis: From aristocratic mastery to slightly chastened but still dominant spectacle-management
matched.overlap_description: Both describe a stable core of aristocratic control and theatrical manipulation, with only a modest shift toward caution and entanglement after their games produce harm.

matched.set_a_axis: From carefree prankery to uneasy moral self-consciousness
matched.set_b_axis: From aristocratic mastery to slightly chastened but still dominant spectacle-management
matched.overlap_description: Both register that the pranks are not wholly harmless; Set A emphasizes moral awareness and unease, while Set B treats this as brief practical caution rather than deep ethical change.

matched.set_a_axis: From harmless connoisseurs to compromised directors
matched.set_b_axis: From aristocratic mastery to slightly chastened but still dominant spectacle-management
matched.overlap_description: Both capture a damaged self-concept: they remain proud directors, but their confidence in being clever, harmless aesthetes is punctured by consequences.

unique_to_a.axis: From entertainment without limits to entertainment with consequences

matched.set_a_axis: From rustic amusement to complicated respect
matched.set_b_axis: From amused patronage to warmer, more engaged amusement
matched.overlap_description: Both describe a warming relation to Sancho: he remains subordinate, but his wit, competence, and moral seriousness force more respect and engagement.

matched.set_a_axis: From co-hosting to conspiratorial partnership
matched.set_b_axis: From aligned co-conspirators to fully synchronized theatrical partners
matched.overlap_description: Both present the Duke and Duchess as a highly aligned pair whose collaboration in spectacle and manipulation remains strong and largely unchanged.

unique_to_a.axis: From managed courtesy to punitive humiliation

unique_to_b.axis: From delighted exploitation to slightly cautious but still exploitative management

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From aristocratic mastery to chastened spectacle-management
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: They begin as socially superior, highly agentic aristocrats who control events from above, treating others as material for amusement and theatrical display.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: They end still dominant and controlling, but more cautious, self-monitoring, and aware that their performances create real harm and entanglement.

trajectory.position_description: They enter as amused directors of the scene, staging hospitality and ceremony while remaining emotionally detached from the people they manipulate.
key_moments: They plan to indulge Don Quixote's delusion
They supervise a lavish ceremonial reception

trajectory.position_description: Their control becomes more collaborative and immersive: they co-author pranks, sustain household theater, and fold Sancho into the spectacle.
key_moments: The Duchess endorses enchantment narratives
They jointly plan and execute new deceptions
Sancho's governorship becomes part of their managed performance

trajectory.position_description: Injury, surprise, and resistance force them to recognize limits; they remain dominant, but their agency is now tempered by practical caution and partial remorse.
key_moments: Don Quixote is injured and they are startled
Sancho proves harder to control than expected
They manage fallout through ceremony and patronage

trajectory.position_description: They settle back into stable hierarchy, but now with a more administrative and self-conscious style of control rather than pure amusement.
key_moments: They continue presiding over staged spectacles
Household discipline replaces open prank escalation

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: The strongest consensus is that their core agency never changes: they remain masters of the social frame. What shifts is the degree of communion and self-awareness embedded in that mastery, which becomes more entangled and cautious after repeated consequences.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From carefree prankery to uneasy moral self-consciousness
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: They begin treating deception as harmless aristocratic entertainment, with little concern for the ethics of exploiting Don Quixote and Sancho.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: They end still manipulating others, but with a more persistent awareness that their games can cause real harm and cannot be fully defended as innocent amusement.

trajectory.position_description: They initially experience the whole affair as witty spectacle; external rebukes do not yet alter their conduct.
key_moments: They plan to indulge Don Quixote for fun
The ecclesiastic condemns their conduct

trajectory.position_description: They begin to recognize the ethical problem, especially the Duchess, but this awareness is absorbed into sophistication and self-justification rather than restraint.
key_moments: The Duchess notes the moral implication of exploiting Sancho
They acknowledge cruelty without stopping

trajectory.position_description: Injury and humiliation make the cruelty harder to deny; they feel shock and regret, though not enough to abandon the pattern.
key_moments: Don Quixote is badly injured
Sancho's battered condition forces recognition of harm
Sancho's dignity sharpens their sense of his seriousness

trajectory.position_description: They do not reform, but they increasingly manage fallout through rescue, provision, and household discipline, showing a residual moral awareness that remains partial and compromised.
key_moments: They organize Sancho's rescue
They offer future provision
They manage Altisidora's distress as a practical problem

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: This axis is one of the clearest internal developments: they do not become virtuous, but they do become harder to imagine as fully innocent pranksters. Moral self-consciousness grows, even if it never defeats their appetite for control.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From harmless connoisseurs to compromised directors
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: They initially see themselves as witty, elegant hosts who can aestheticize absurdity and remain above the moral consequences.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: They end as still-proud orchestrators, but with a damaged self-image: they know their cleverness has produced real suffering and unpredictable consequences.

trajectory.position_description: They imagine themselves as refined connoisseurs of romance and ceremony, capable of turning reality into tasteful entertainment.
key_moments: They plan the encounter as controlled social theater
They see themselves as directors of an elaborate reception

trajectory.position_description: Their self-concept hardens into that of expert manipulators and stage-managers, reinforced by successful deceptions and the apparent pliability of others.
key_moments: Don Quixote's elaborate reasoning delights them
The Clavileño deception confirms their stage-manager identity
Sancho's governorship becomes a gratifying spectacle

trajectory.position_description: Injury, surprise, and Sancho's competence puncture their self-image. They preserve pride, but the fantasy of harmless cleverness is no longer secure.
key_moments: Don Quixote's injury shocks them
Sancho proves unexpectedly capable
They realize the experiment is harder to control

trajectory.position_description: They recover by reframing themselves as benevolent patrons and careful managers, preserving status while softening the appearance of cruelty.
key_moments: They promise Sancho another post
The Duke preserves illusion rather than confronting fraud
The Duchess acts as household arbiter

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Their self-image changes less in kind than in stability. They remain proud directors of the spectacle, but the novel steadily exposes the cost of that identity, leaving it more defensive and less innocent.

intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From entertainment without limits to entertainment with consequences
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: They treat pranks as self-justifying courtly play, where wit and elegance excuse manipulation.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: They increasingly recognize that spectacle can produce bodily harm, social disruption, and moral residue, even if they still continue to enjoy it.

trajectory.position_description: Early pranks are experienced as clever, bounded, and harmless; their pleasure depends on the assumption that the game is only a game.
key_moments: They delight in Sancho's wit at table
They resolve to continue the joke

trajectory.position_description: Repeated moral pressure and physical harm make the costs of the game harder to deny. Their amusement persists, but it is increasingly contaminated by awareness of damage.
key_moments: The Duchess briefly acknowledges cruelty
Don Quixote is badly injured
The Duchess turns insult into revenge
Sancho's battered exit forces regret

trajectory.position_description: They do not renounce spectacle, but they become more careful about framing, rescue, and patronage. Entertainment is now shadowed by the need to manage fallout.
key_moments: They rescue Sancho from the pit
They offer a new post
They redirect Altisidora's distress into needlework

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: This axis captures the gradual contamination of amusement by consequence. It is best retained as a distinct event-driven refinement of their moral awareness and self-image.

relational_axes.axis_name: From amused hospitality to controlled patronage
relational_axes.pole_start: They begin with playful curiosity and performative hospitality, treating Don Quixote as an entertaining curiosity whom they can safely indulge.
relational_axes.pole_end: They end as still-courteous but clearly controlling patrons who manage his departures, beliefs, and humiliations while preserving the appearance of respect.

trajectory.position_description: Their relation starts as amused welcome: they embrace him, stage ceremonies, and treat him as a living romance figure.
key_moments: They plan to indulge his knight-errantry
They stage a lavish ceremonial reception

trajectory.position_description: They move from hospitality to active orchestration. Don Quixote becomes the center of a managed fantasy in which they direct his interpretations and responses.
key_moments: His defense of Dulcinea confirms his delusion
The Duchess endorses the enchantment narrative
They stage the nighttime deception
They engineer the Clavileño flight

trajectory.position_description: Their relation remains exploitative, but injuries, surprises, and improvisations reveal that their control is not absolute. They continue to manage him, now with more awareness of risk.
key_moments: Don Quixote is injured and they feel remorse
The Duke stages himself as arbiter of justice
Tosilos's refusal destabilizes the script
The Duke preserves the illusion rather than confronting it

trajectory.position_description: They end by framing his departure as gracious and by continuing to manage his image from a distance. The relationship remains hierarchical, but the overt prank cycle is winding down.
key_moments: They perform regret at his leaving
The Duchess still treats him as a subject of observation

relational_axes.evidence_summary: This is the central relationship arc: it moves from amused hospitality to sustained manipulation, with occasional flashes of concern that never undo the asymmetry. Respect is mostly ceremonial; control is the stable endpoint.

relational_axes.axis_name: From amused patronage to warmer, more engaged amusement
relational_axes.pole_start: They begin with superficial amusement and low esteem, treating Sancho as a comic subordinate useful for entertainment.
relational_axes.pole_end: They end still patronizing him, but with noticeably warmer appreciation for his wit, bargaining, and verbal resourcefulness.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho is first treated as a lively subordinate and comic foil; they are amused by him but still clearly above him.
key_moments: They show interest in Sancho as comic wit
They enjoy his improprieties and verbal boldness

trajectory.position_description: They increasingly flatter and engage Sancho, valuing his intelligence and proverbs as part of the performance while still controlling him.
key_moments: They actively cultivate Sancho’s trust
They use his reactions and letters as entertainment

trajectory.position_description: They remain amused by his governorship and practical resistance, showing a warmer surface regard but no real equality.
key_moments: Barataria mock government unfolds
They continue the joke despite unintended harm
They manage him from afar through letters

trajectory.position_description: They continue to find him entertaining and useful, with the Duchess especially showing performative friendliness and the Duke treating him as a comic subject worth managing.
key_moments: The Duchess sends gifts and letters to Teresa Panza
